lesson.title: What Makes an Equation Linear: The One-Variable Family
lesson.summary: Define a linear equation in one variable precisely, distinguish it from equations with higher powers, and preview why this family always has zero, one, or infinitely many solutions.
lesson.body:
Throughout this unit, every equation solved (one-step, multi-step, with variables on both sides, with fractions or decimals) has belonged to the same family: a linear equation in one variable. This is an equation that can be written, after simplifying, in the form ax + b = c, where x is the only variable, and that variable appears only to the first power, never squared, cubed, or under a root, and never multiplied by itself or by another variable. The word linear comes from the fact that if you were to graph y = ax + b, the result is a straight line; an equation restricts that line to the single point where it crosses a particular height.

Recognizing what makes an equation linear matters because the solving method depends on it. An equation like x^2 = 9 is not linear, since x is squared, and it generally has two solutions instead of one. An equation like 1/x = 4 is not linear either, since x appears in a denominator. But an equation like 7x - 3 = 2x + 12, even though it looks complicated with terms on both sides, is linear, because every x in it is a plain, first-power x; the properties of equality used throughout this unit apply because of that structure.

The formal name for this comes from the exponent on the variable: a linear equation in one variable always has degree 1, meaning the highest power of x present is 1. An equation with degree 2, such as x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0, is called quadratic instead, and it is generally solved with different methods, including factoring or the quadratic formula, that produce up to two solutions rather than one. Knowing the degree of an equation before starting is a quick way to confirm that the linear methods in this unit, and not some other method, are the right tool for the job.

Solve 7x - 3 = 2x + 12 to see the full linear-equation process in one place. Subtract 2x from both sides to gather variable terms: 5x - 3 = 12. Add 3 to both sides: 5x = 15. Divide both sides by 5: x = 3. Check by substituting x = 3 into the original equation: the left side is 7(3) - 3 = 21 - 3 = 18, and the right side is 2(3) + 12 = 6 + 12 = 18. Both sides equal 18, confirming x = 3.

This whole process rests on the meaning of a variable as a placeholder standing for one specific unknown number, the value that makes the equation a true statement. For a linear equation in one variable, there are exactly three possible outcomes once it is fully simplified: it settles on one specific value of x, like the x = 3 found above, it turns out to be true for every possible value of x, or it turns out to be true for no value of x at all. These three outcomes, called conditional equations, identities, and contradictions, are examined individually next, since being able to recognize which one you are looking at is as important as being able to solve for x.

Every technique built in this unit, clearing fractions, clearing decimals, collecting variables from both sides, exists to take an equation and reduce it down to this same standard linear form, ax + b = c, because once an equation is in that shape, the solving process is always the same short sequence of inverse operations.
